utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Today is scheduled, I believe, was a Pre-Trial Conference, and I would invite Judge Harhoff, who has been intimately involved with the details of this matter for a long time to take over at this point in terms of leading today's proceedings. Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I start by asking the Registrar to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-PT, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And I would like the parties to present themselves for the hearing today. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of the Prosecution it's Joanna Korner, Thomas Hannis, and Alexis Demirdjian. In my jurisdiction it is traditional that when there are new Judges the Prosecution says something. Can we say on behalf of the OTP how delighted we are to see Judge Hall and Judge Delvoie, and we hope that we will find the case an interesting one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Korner. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Mr. Stanisic's Defence appearing are Slobodan Zecevic, as a lead counsel; to my left is my colleague, Mr. Slobodan Cvijetic; to my right is also my colleague Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan; and our case manager, Tatjana Savic. I would also like to extend my congratulations to the appointment of the Judges to this Tribunal. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Zecevic. And for the Defence of Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Igor Pantelic, lead counsel for Mr. Zupljanin. Next to me is my learned friend and colleague Mr. Dragan Krgovic, my co-counsel; and our legal assistant, Mr. Brent Hicks; and our case manager, Mr. Eric Tully. I also would like on behalf of Zupljanin Defence team to wish a very warm welcome to newly appointed Judges, and we hope that we should have a fair and good trial here. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Pantelic, for your warm wishes. And for the part of the Court we would like to welcome everyone in and around the courtroom, and also good afternoon to the two accused, to whom I would like to put the question if they can understand what we say in a language that is being interpreted to them. THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] Yes, we do. Thank you. I do understand. THE ACCUSED ZUPLJANIN: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zupljanin. Sorry, I'm not sure that your response was recorded. Can you please tell me again if you can understand what I'm saying. You have to press the button in front of you. There you go. THE ACCUSED ZUPLJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, I hope that you didn't switch it off now. Yes, you didn't. Yes, I understand you, Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, and I understand everything that's being said and I wish you the best of luck in your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And we wish you a good trial, both of you. Now, we have for the purpose of the Pre-Trial Conference today issued an agenda, which I hope has been distributed to everyone, including the accused. I don't know if they have a copy. They have. And so as you can see there are a few points that are included in the agenda, but before we start the discussions I would like to ask if any of the parties have any other matters which they wish to have included in today's agenda. For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think at this stage on the face of it there's nothing I wish to add. It's simply we're not altogether clear about what some of the headings are going to cover and I think we'll wait and see what's going to be covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very good. And of course you may wish any question you have at the end when we get to the end. If there's anything that hasn't been covered of what you wanted to have covered, then please raise it at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We don't have anything to add to existing agenda. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Not for the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Let's get on with it, then. The first thing we would wish to raise from the Bench is the motion that was filed last night by Mr. Zecevic for postponement of the trial. Mr. Zecevic included limited resources available to the Defence, late disclosure by the Prosecution, and possible violations of a right to a fair trial as the three reasons for which the Stanisic Defence team wishes to delay the opening of the trial. The Chamber should hear the Prosecution's view on this before we render our decision on the Defence motion. If you have a view on this, Mrs. Korner, we would like to hear it right away; otherwise, we would invite you to do in writing very quickly and urgently. Monday, by noon, if possible. But if you can do it orally at this moment it would be good. And I'll tell you the reason why we're pushing forward with this decision is that we want all these matters to be cleared and settled well in advance of the opening of the trial, which is in ten days. And so the sooner we can render this decision the better. The Registrar -- sorry, the Registrar has already advised that they would wish to make a submission under Rule 33(B) also by Monday, and the Chamber will then proceed to hand down its decision on Tuesday. So if you can, we would be very pleased if you would present your views either today orally or, at the latest, Monday, midday, in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I put it this way: We are not unsympathetic to the problems raised by Mr. Zecevic, of which we of course were not aware as the Prosecution, namely, the lack of resources that he has referred to. We do reject and will answer allegations that it is in any way the fault of the Prosecution, but the length of the motion, Your Honour, as you will see, means that in order to respond properly we will have to put it in writing. But if overall this were to be dealt with on the basis of the resources which Mr. Zecevic has complained about, the Prosecution is not unsympathetic to the problems, we would say that ten weeks which has been asked for is too long, but we would not oppose a shorter adjournment. That is effectively what we'll be saying. But if Your Honours were to be minded to take into account and look at the various allegations that are being made that this is any way the fault of the Prosecution, then we will have to put in a full reply. Your Honours, Monday is really very soon, but we are dealing with endless motions at the moment which have been coming our way. And to be able to respond fully, if that's what Your Honour wants, we would certainly ask for Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Korner. I think the view of the Chamber is that, you know, we wouldn't require you to respond in any length. I think we understand the gist of your response. If you wish to add anything to what you have said, you can do so briefly by Monday, but I think the earlier we take the decision the better. And to postpone it much beyond Tuesday, I think, is simply not wise. Let's get clear of this issue as soon as we can so that we are ready at the latest by Tuesday --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- to know whether or not we will go to trial next week --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, can I add this: In particular the reason that we're, as I say, not objecting in principle to a shorter adjournment, apart from Mr. Zecevic's and his team's problems, is that at the moment we still -- we don't know yet what form our evidence is going to take in the sense of who will be a 92 bis, who will be a 92 ter. And therefore, to that extent, say an adjournment of a week or two weeks, would probably assist us because then we'll be able to work on the ruling that we're given. So can I just add that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Certainly. So you may decide over the weekend whether you wish to add anything in writing, but if you do so then --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- the order is set for Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honour, what we don't want is for the suggestion to remain on the record unanswered by us, that the delay is through the fault of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have understood that. Thanks. The next issue that we thought we should address head on is the overriding issue of the time and the number of witnesses that will be available to the Prosecution at trial. The Chamber has considered the issue very carefully and we have included a number of considerations in our deliberations, such as the official functions of the two accused; the number of counts, charges, in the indictment; the gravity of the crimes; the number of victims; the number of municipalities and the geographical scope of the indictment, it's about 20 municipalities which is a large part; the time span, nine months in 1992, covered by the indictment; and of course the right of the accused to a fair and to an expeditious trial as well as the Prosecution's right to be given adequate time to present its evidence. The Prosecution has asked for 292 hours net to present its evidence. To this number the Chamber would have to grant at least the same number of hours for Defence to cross-examine. And as you know, the practice here is that we would then on top of that have to add another 20 per cent for procedural matters, questions by the Judges, re-examination, and other such things. That would bring us up to all together - I can't remember how much - but the length of the trial would be depending on the fact that the Prosecution's case will then take approximately a year if that were to be granted. The Prosecution has also called or sought to call 162 witnesses and to present those witnesses -- present the evidence from those witnesses in one or another form during those 292 hours which they have applied for. As I said, the Chamber has very carefully examined these numbers and taken into consideration the factors that I lined out just a while ago. During the pre-trial stage of the case, I as the Pre-Trial Judge announced that I would suggest to the Trial Chamber 180 hours, and this was following earlier and intense discussions which we had at the 65 ter meetings for trying to see if it was possible to narrow down the scope of the Prosecution's case. In spite of my many recommendations and before me the earlier Pre-Trial Judge's invitations to the Prosecution to delimit the scope of the case and despite numerous assertions by the various Prosecution teams that they would indeed do so, it seems to me that what has in effect happened is that the number of hours and the number of witnesses had at least sometimes been increased. In any case, be that as it may, I return to now what the Chamber's determination of the number of hours and the number of victim -- witnesses should be. The Chamber is unanimous in its order that the Prosecution be given 212 hours. This would bring us to Easter. In fact, we had seen if it would be possible to adjourn a week or two before the Easter holiday, but we wanted to give the Prosecution as much relief as we could. So the number of 212 hours is final and that will bring us to just before the Easter break - I think it is on 1st of April, 2010 - and this calculation is done by using the method that I described just a while ago, that the Prosecution has 212 hours, the Defence will all together be given the same amount of time, 212 hours; and then we add the 20 per cent for procedural matters and we end up approximately at 508 or 509 hours all together for the Prosecution's presentation of its evidence. This does not, as I have included earlier, cover time for opening and closing arguments. That is added. So there it is: 25 weeks you have to present the evidence in your case. As for the number of witnesses, we have gone through each and every single statement that the Prosecution has submitted to us and we have looked at most of the material that pertains to these witnesses. We have noticed that a number of the statements and the testimonies given by some of these witnesses appears to be really very repetitive or redundant, as you might say. This is why we suggest that the Prosecution once again, in light of the number of witnesses which we will allow, reconsider the witness list to see if it is possible to knock off some of the witnesses whose testimony or statements or whose evidence would appear to be redundant. We will order the Prosecution to bring 131 witnesses. And we -- in doing so, we are careful not to try and control the Prosecution's case. So we will not seek to tell you which witnesses you should knock off, but if I can use a few examples just for your illustration, I will say that in your witness list as far as the 92 bis witnesses are concerned - and those are the witnesses who will not appear ordinarily in court live but whose testimony or whose statement will be admitted on paper only - the Prosecution has proposed I think it's about 35, 92 bis witnesses. If we look at the list and we read the statements of the 92 bis witnesses who are sought to be admitted for Brcko, it would be our view that the evidence to be offered by Witness ST1 and ST2 seems to us to be really overlapping, repetitive, and redundant. We suggest, but it's not -- it's just an example that we give you in order to show you how we have arrived at the number of 131 witnesses, we would suggest that you knock off either ST1 or ST2, but you don't need to bring both of them. The same, for instance, just to take another example of the 92 bis witnesses which you have proposed for Ilijas, the evidence offered by Witness ST4 and ST51 again appears to us to be redundant. We would suggest you consider knocking off either one or the other but don't bring both of them. Similarly for the 92 bis witnesses that are suggested for Pale, what Witness ST56 [sic], 60, and 61 have to say seems to us to be very overlapping. Why don't you consider knocking off either one or both, or two of the three. These are examples, Ms. Korner, and I don't want to be seen to -- I don't want you to understand that the Chamber is in any way - please sit down - interfering with the way that you should put together your witness list. But we give you some reasons why we have arrived at this lower number. For the 92 ter group, we have identified at least 10, 11 witnesses whose testimony appears to be subsumed either in what you have proposed as adjudicated facts or, more importantly, more importantly, by the testimony of other witnesses. So here again in our view there is ample room to reconsider if you want to bring all of these witnesses or can reduce your witnesses -- witness list by a number. As for the viva voce, we also have looked at it and some of the witnesses appears -- appear to us to be not necessary, some because it's -- their testimony appears to be irrelevant to the case, some because it's repetitive, and particularly in relation to -- this goes for at least six, seven of the witnesses that you have proposed to call viva voce, and particularly in relation to ST107 and ST201 and ST158. We don't think that their evidence is relevant at all. It doesn't concern any material in the case. And we would suggest you knock them off. I'm unaware of whether any protective measures applies to these witnesses. I don't think so, but I would not state their names. But you have the pseudonyms. So all together this leads us to the assumption that the Prosecution could, without suffering any harm to their case, easily knock off some 35, 40 witnesses from their list, and thus that brings us down to the number of 131 witnesses that we have suggested. It goes without saying, but I'm -- this is not an invitation to apply for -- to apply for addition of more time or inclusion of other witnesses on your list at a later stage, but of course this opportunity remains open anyway. But we would say that the Prosecution can, without any harm to its case, present the evidence in 212 hours through the testimony of 131 witnesses in this case. So that is the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Your Honour moves on, in respect of the 92 bis witnesses, of course 92 bis means they won't be called to give evidence and therefore no time is used up by their evidence. And Your Honour has suggested, however, that we should be dispensing with some witnesses, examples of which have been given. If it doesn't affect the time, then I'm not quite clear, even though I appreciate what Your Honours say, why we should be removing witnesses which obviously we've included because we think they're important for an issue. That's the only question I'm raising at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I suppose your question relates to the 92 bis witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, only to the 92 bis. I understand the others that Your Honour is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Our suggestion for the 92 bis witnesses, Mrs. Korner, is put forward to you out of the simple principle that the Prosecution, and the Defence when it comes to their case, are bound to focus their case and only bring the necessary evidence. So in our view, you don't have to bring, even if it's on paper, you don't have to bring the evidence of four or five witnesses if they all say the same thing. 92 bis witnesses anyway are witnesses that are corroborating other oral evidence typically. So they are in the lower end of the evidence chain anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So even though we are fully aware of the fact that of course they don't take up any time, we still don't think that you need to bring them. Focus your case. That's what we are asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I imagine -- I wanted to hear what Your Honour's reasoning behind that was. And, Your Honour, can I take it that the limitation on hours and witnesses has been taken notwithstanding the motion that we filed on the 31st of August in respect of why we felt this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, no, that has been taken into consideration. Now, on the basis of these findings - you may sit down -- do you understand -- do you have more to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I haven't. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm inviting you to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm standing while you're talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, you don't have to. On the basis of these findings, we would invite -- or order -- sorry, order the Prosecution to file its revised final witness list by noon on the 10th of September, which is Thursday, next week. So you have a couple of days to reshuffle and put forward a final revised witness list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- can I say that we would prefer to have more time to consider what is a really important matter from the point of view of the Prosecution. One of the difficulties that we've had is that as yet we have no clear idea, if any idea, of what the issues in the case are likely to be from the Defence responses to the pre-trial brief, as we made clear. To ask us by the 10th of September, before we start the trial, to remove 40-odd witnesses is, in our view, something we would prefer to have considerably more time to look at, and in particular where we've got viva voce witnesses. 10th of December [sic], we would respectfully submit, is too soon, in particular with everything else that we have to deal with that has come in from the Defence, as we made clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand your point. Now, the Defence, on their side, they need to be put on notice before the trial starts who are the witnesses that are going to come. Now, I will consult with my colleagues whether we can find a middle way perhaps to say that you have to indicate at least the first 20 witnesses for the -- that will enable the Defence to prepare at least for those -- the first batch of witnesses and then you may supply the remaining witnesses towards the end -- after that, if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. We're perfectly prepared to do that and will do that. Can I say that we've already indicated who the first two witnesses are, but one of the reasons why - can I put it this way? - matters are becoming complicated in this trial is that recently a motion has been filed objecting in full to the first two witnesses in this case because they're experts and it's alleged they're not experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Mrs. Korner, I understood that the -- or maybe I should address myself to the Defence. The objection that you have raised against the two first witnesses, expert witnesses, I think it's Robert Donia and Christian Nielsen. Is that correct? Your objection against Nielsen was that his reports or his latest reports hadn't been translated into B/C/S yet. So the indication from the translation services, CLSS, was that this couldn't be done until sometime in November, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's being disclosed, Your Honour, this week. That's not the objection. The objection is they're not experts. There's a huge motion, I don't know whether Your Honour has seen it, which came from Mr. Zecevic a couple of days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Zecevic, you better explain to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very shortly. It is indeed the case that we filed a motion. It's a motion filed on the 31st of August, it's Mico Stanisic supplemental filing in response to the Prosecution's filing on proposed experts in response to the Prosecution supplemental motion for admission of the evidence of experts pursuant to Rules 94 bis, 92 bis and 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I extend my apology to the translators. Evidence of experts pursuant to Rules 94 bis, 92 bis and 92 ter with confidential annexes. It was filed 31st of August, 2009. There are two different categories of the experts. We have objected to five experts, namely, Mr. Christian Nielsen, Patrick Treanor, Dorothea Hanson, Ewan Brown, and Ewa Tabeau. Among other things, our objection is based on the fact that all these five are the employees of the Prosecution and they're working in the Prosecution team. That is -- that goes for these five experts. In respect of Robert Donia and other experts of the Prosecution, like Dr. Riedlmayer, Robert Donia, and so on, our objection was on the supplemental filing of their expert report. We didn't question their -- their ability to present -- to appear here as experts. We were just commenting and objecting to the late disclosure of their supplemental expert reports. So there is a difference between the two categories of the experts in our filing. So therefore, if I may conclude, it -- in practice it means that we are objecting on Mr. Robert Donia introducing his supplemental expert report, but we are not objecting for him appearing here on his original report. On the other hand, we are objecting to Mr. Christian Nielsen for the reasons why we -- which we stated in our motion. I hope I have been of assistance to the Trial Chamber. What I'm trying to say is that therefore the suggestion that this is aimed at the prolongation and -- of the start of the trial is not -- is not right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. As I understand, your objection against Donia is that basically the supplement was filed so late that you didn't have a chance to take it into account; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly the case, Your Honours, plus that that part of the report we received the translation, as my learned friend from the Prosecution said, just yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you received only the last part of it yesterday? Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah -- well, this supplemental report which was received which we objected to was received only in English. We received the translations only yesterday of that part of the report of Mr. Donia, but we objected to it anyhow as a late disclosure, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And when did you receive the supplement in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just -- please bear with me, Your Honour. I believe it was couple of weeks ago. I cannot -- at this moment I cannot find the right date, but my colleague will try to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're checking. We think it was in July sometime, but we're just checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, thanks for this. And can I just, to be sure, ask you your objections against Christian Nielsen was -- other than the fact that the English -- the B/C/S translations came in only yesterday, other than that do you have any other objections against Nielsen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The objections against Mr. Nielsen are contained in our motion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, that he was a former OTP employee, that that's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that he was a former OTP employee and some other objections which you will see from the arguments in our motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But as far as Mr. Nielsen is concerned, there was no problem with the translation of his report. It has been disclosed some time ago. It is the other question concerning translation with Mr. Nielsen. It is the problem that we are facing with the CLSS in translation of the Defence documents, which we would like to show during the cross-examination. But I believe that's point 7 on the agenda, but if Your Honour -- if it pleases the Court we can discuss it right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We'll come to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Point 7. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just to assist my learned colleague and also Trial Chamber, actually we are speaking about the supplement part of Dr. Donia report, not Mr. Nielsen. So actually we received only English translation of Dr. Donia report, and only yesterday we received B/C/S translation, which of course, Your Honour, in accordance with the Rules and the well-established case law here, it's out of the standards for disclosure because we have to confer with our clients. We have to get instructions, and so on. So just for the record this is a case for Dr. Donia report, not Mr. Nielsen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, I have -- the Chamber has fully understood that as for Donia, it's the translation into B/C/S of the supplement, and for Christian Nielsen it's the other way around, it's the translation into English of some of the documents that the Stanisic Defence wishes to put forward during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- we just identified when it was filed by the Prosecution. It is the Prosecution's supplemental motion for admission of the evidence of experts pursuant to Rules 94 bis, 92 bis, and 92 ter with confidential annexes dated 14 of August. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, can I -- it was disclosed to the Defence in English on the 8th of July, 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I return to -- I don't know what decision Your Honour's taken, but Your Honour can see that, at the moment, with matters as they stand and with the number of motions we still have to deal with, we ask that Your Honours don't ask us to make a major decision, such as the removal of 40 witnesses from our list, at this stage. We will certainly provide advance notice at the very least immediately of the first ten witnesses we propose to call subject to rulings on the various motions to preclude the evidence. And the second matter is this, Your Honour, Your Honour says we need to remove 92 bis, 92 ter, et cetera, and we still don't know which they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, that's exactly what the Chamber did not say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Your Honour suggested that there were witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Chamber invited you to re-draw your witness list so as to end at a total number of 131. Now, if you wish to have all those 131 witnesses as 92 bis witnesses you can do so. If you wish to have all of them as viva voce, you can do so. We just provided you with a few examples in order just to illustrate how the Chamber had reached its conclusion as to the number of 131 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you can put together the witness list any way you wish, but there is, as I have indicated to you, room for weeding out repetitive evidence in all three categories.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, may I just add one other thing because it's really a question of -- it's the relationship of witnesses and hours. Once we know which witnesses we may call through the procedure 92 bis, in other words, not have them here for cross-examination, likewise 92 quater, you can't cross-examine them, but whether those are admissible, then of course it at least gives us the beginnings of to know where to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I appreciate that, and I apologise for omitting the one part of our decision, namely, that all the 92 bis witnesses that you have proposed can, in our view, be called as 92 bis witnesses. They all fulfil the requirements, and so in respect of the Defence objections to it that part is overruled. We find that the -- that the 92 bis witnesses can be called, except -- except two -- yes, sorry, I was too quick. utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me provide you with some of the thoughts that went through the Chamber's heads when we drew up this scheme. The principle in Rule 94 bis is that the calling party presents the expert's report. That is the basic substance of the expert evidence. Now, the other party can then indicate whether they accept the expert witness as an expert and whether they accept his report or her report; and if they don't, they can call the expert witness for cross-examination. That's the system. So in principle, the rule doesn't foresee that an expert be examined in chief. Now, the practice of this Tribunal is that very frequently the experts are, indeed, examined in chief. Please. And we looked actually at all the experts that the Prosecution has sought to call to see how long time they were examined for in chief in other cases before this Tribunal. And there is obviously a difference between the expert witnesses -- between the time for which the expert witnesses were examined in chief. Those expert witnesses who normally provide general background are, in fact, only examined in chief normally in this case by the Prosecution because we looked at the Prosecution's expert witnesses -- only examined in chief by the Prosecution for an hour or two, some even less, right down to I think one expert report -- expert was examined in chief only for 16 minutes. Whereas the experts who provide -- experts to the substance of the case, such as military experts or experts in other fields other than general background information, that they tend to be examined for a much longer time in chief by the Prosecution. On that information we thought that it was wise to set out a general rule, according to which the calling party would have one hour to present the expert, to give a little background about his or her curriculum vitae, and possibly to introduce some of the documents that pertain to the report, because in the tail of each expert report there's always a number of other documents that follow. So we would provide the calling party with time to introduce the witness, to introduce those supplementary documents that go with it, but that's basically it; and then we would expect the other party to cross-examine. And for each expert witness we would then set the maximum time for -- in this case for the Defence for its cross-examination of the expert witnesses. Now, we are fully aware of the fact that people such as, for instance, Robert Donia might -- that the Prosecution might wish to examine him in chief for a longer time, which is why in the procedural guide-lines we then said, Okay, if the Prosecution wishes to deviate from this general rule, it can apply for leave. And so we thought it was -- the better system is to simply set down a general rule, which is one hour for the calling party, and then if for any good reason the calling party can convince the Chamber that it is necessary for the benefit of the Chamber itself - because we are the ones who benefit from the testimony of the experts - if we would like actually to have the calling party lead the evidence -- lead the witness through his report at a -- you know, in an extended time we would grant that. But otherwise, if we were able to read and understand the expert report, we don't see any reason why the calling party should have more time. So it's -- it boils down to the issue of whether the Chamber is immediately able to appreciate the evidence that is given in the expert report. If we think that we can understand it, we can grasp it, then we don't see any reason why the calling party should have more than an hour. If, on the other hand, we find that the information provided in the expert reports is such that we have a difficulty simply in understanding what this is about, then of course we would expect the calling party to use more time in introducing the expert report through the expert. That's the reasoning behind this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But I would hope that we receive that in writing, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay, thank you very much. Now, as concerning Nielsen, if the case is that he will be appearing as a witness, I think probably the best -- the best solution would be that he's the -- our colleagues conduct the cross-examination and then the -- I mean the direct examination, I'm sorry, and then the cross-examination is conducted once we have the documents.
