Now, what we are -- I think that's probably the best solution since Mr. Nielsen is in the building at --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry -- I'm sorry -- well, yeah -- but in that case I think that is the way how we can proceed, that he's called back and then we can do the cross-examination once we have the documents and then we can proceed on that basis. That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to be helpful. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And you are indeed being very helpful and I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Korner, the situation is this: You can choose either to call Donia right away and then halfway through we'll have to send him back, and then we'll re-call him in a couple of months. And as for Nielsen, the Defence has agreed that you can start out with the introduction of him and whatever examination you wish to do within an hour or, by our leave, more time, and then again for him also we'll have to cut him off when you're through with that so as to allow for the Defence to introduce -- to begin their cross-examination upon reception of the English versions of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two things, Your Honour. The first is, although it's not the most desirable way of proceeding, we accept that Your Honours ruled that that's what's going to happen, so we will call Dr. Donia and then Mr. Nielsen -- Dr. Nielsen. The reason, I think, is because effectively for Your Honours to understand the evidence to be called you have to see the context particularly through Dr. Nielsen. Can I just direct Your Honours, first of all, to Rule 14, Rule -- sorry, guide-line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, please, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as we understand the ruling, the cross-examining party doesn't have to provide copies of the documents it's going to use until the witness is actually being sworn, made the solemn declaration. That may be all very well in some cases, but to receive 432 witnesses -- documents only at the moment the witness goes into the witness box, admittedly in this case because of the gap we'll have slightly more time to look at it, may cause some problems, not only to the Court but obviously to the Prosecution. If these are documents we've never clapped eyes on before in our life, we have no idea whether they're admissible or not, what they are, and we don't get them until the moment the witness comes into the witness box and then has a limited time to give evidence in chief, we're straight into cross-examination, and nobody's had the chance to look at the documents. So I'm merely flagging that up, if I may, as a rule that Your Honours may want to -- as a guide-line that perhaps might be flexible, if I can put it that way. In respect of the time allowed, can I deal with that straightaway. We would ask for more time than one hour for both Dr. Donia and, in particular, Mr. Nielsen. Perhaps less so with Dr. Donia, although we'd worked on the basis that we would have three hours to highlight some of the major aspects of things. With Mr. -- Dr. Nielsen, I keep -- I must beg his pardon for this, we put down seven hours. We will reduce that, but we would certainly wish to have at least -- Mr. Hannis, I think, is in a better position - three hours for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So three hours for both?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Three hours for both, yes -- for each of them, sorry, for each of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think we will wish to have a look at, again, the reports as we know them by now, but -- and we will hand our ruling hopefully by Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just say in respect of Dr. Nielsen, I know Your Honours have had a look at it, it's a very, very dense report indeed and you may well be assisted by hearing from him a little longer than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We had him in mind when we established the system that we have here in the procedural guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, and I'm so sorry. The third witness is likely to be Mr. Treanor. He's also on the -- the list of witnesses -- experts to whom the Defence object and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Patrick it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KORNER
utterances.text: Patrick Treanor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There are two Treanors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, yes. Not the other Treanor, Dr. Treanor. Again, Your Honours, we would be grateful for a ruling in respect of him, whether Your Honours accept him as an expert as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Korner. You will get our ruling next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm helpfully reminded by Mr. Smith, our case manager, whom I completely forgot to introduce to Your Honours, I'm very sorry about that, that if there's no cross-examination of Dr. Donia or Christian Nielsen, then he's likely to be on very quickly, in fact, possibly in the first week, Mr. Treanor -- Dr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. I understand. We're -- we will hear -- Dr. Donia will be the first witness to appear and he will then appear on Wednesday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I don't think -- said -- gave item 2 was the -- item 3 was time for opening statements, but Your Honours are going to give me Monday and Tuesday sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We agreed at the 65 ter meetings that you would use up all of Monday and half of Tuesday's session for --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Possibly a little longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And then if the Defence wishes to provide any preliminary response, then we can do that for Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, the Defence for Stanisic will reserve that right for the beginning of the Defence case. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's what I thought. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Same position with Zupljanin Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. Well, that's it then. Donia will appear Wednesday, I can't remember whether it's Monday morning or -- Wednesday morning or afternoon, as the first witness, and he will --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- on Thursday -- thank you. Dr. Nielsen is the second on Thursday and then that would mean Mr. Treanor on Friday -- Dr. Treanor on Friday. If we're sitting five days that week, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I might have missed something, but it was my understanding that your ruling was that Mr. Donia will be cross-examined on the basis of his first report and not on the basis of the supplemental report and only will be re-called to be cross-examined and present the supplemental report. So therefore it might be that he is in -- he goes into Thursday as well. So just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I fully agree and I was just about to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- to say exactly that; namely, that if the Defence wants to begin its cross-examination of Dr. Donia on the basis of his previous reports but not, obviously, on the basis of the Karadzic supplement, then the Defence is free to do so. And my understanding, if I understand you correctly, Mr. Zecevic, is that you will indeed wish to begin your cross-examination of Dr. Donia on the basis of his previous material --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we haven't consulted, but I -- I'm -- as far as the Stanisic Defence at least, because I haven't had time to consult with my colleagues, the Stanisic Defence will definitely conduct the cross-examination of Dr. Donia on the basis of the first report. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That makes perfect sense. Thank you. For the purpose of assessing how much time we would need for Dr. Donia, Mr. Pantelic, can you indicate at this point whether you also would wish to begin your cross-examination of Dr. Donia already at this point or would you reserve your bullets for his re-appearance?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Dr. Donia's report doesn't have any relevance to my client and especially this supplement for Karadzic because my understanding is that it covers Sarajevo area which is absolutely irrelevant to my client. Regarding the option for cross-examination, I must confer with my learned friends from Stanisic Defence so that we could possibly arrange or re-arrange our way of cross-examination and the timing. And then we can accordingly inform the Chamber about exact time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour, before we leave that -- the wonders of e-mail. The experts that we've been talking about are witnesses in other cases, one of which is going on at the moment. I've had a request that came up in the Stanisic/Simatovic case, too, in a different context, that Your Honours make a ruling that other trial teams may speak to the witnesses in between examination-in-chief and the cross, if it's to be delayed or, for example, in Dr. Donia, he still awaits cross-examination. Because the normal rule is, of course, that you can't talk to a witness until he's concluded his evidence. Can I just raise that with Your Honours to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know that the Trial Chamber in the Stanisic/Simatovic case is dealing with -- grappling with the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Where is Dr. Donia at the moment? Is he here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, he's in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider it. We still have one hot issue to debate under point 7 of the agenda, and that is the joint Defence motion to preclude the witnesses and exhibits that came in late. We have grappled with that issue for quite some time, and our position is this: Ordinarily the final witness lists and the final list of exhibits according to Rule 65 ter should have been submitted along with the pre-trial brief, and we assume that that had taken place. That's the way we read the rule, 65 ter (E). When at the subsequent 65 ter meeting which we held with the parties we discovered that still disclosure was ongoing, we then hurried to issue a new decision, saying that the Prosecution would have to submit its witness list and its list of exhibits by 31st July, and that -- and that would be according to Rule 66(A)(ii), and that the Prosecution would be required to seek the Chamber's leave in case any disclosure of this material would have to be made after that date. I think this was clear and there is no other way to read it in the transcript of that 65 ter meeting. We then met again in the 65 ter meeting in August, after the recess, I think it was the 24th of August, and there the Defence drew our attention to the fact that disclosure was still ongoing. And by the Prosecution's own admission, some 74 documents apparently had still not been disclosed for a number of reasons. We then asked the Prosecution to specify exactly the reasons why this had not been done and which witnesses it would affect in case the Trial Chamber were to find that because of the late disclosure this material could not be admitted into evidence. In your response that came last week, I think, you said that in fact it was not 74 documents, it was only 50 documents and that, in your view, the Defence would not suffer any prejudice from the late disclosure of this material mainly because of the fact that you were not intending to make any use of it anyway. So you did not intend to include those 50 documents in your 65 ter list of exhibits anyway. That's what -- that's how we understood it. Now, if we resume the entire story of this issue of late disclosure, the Chamber's view is that by virtue of my decision as Pre-Trial Judge some time in July, I think it was the 8th of July, 7th of July, I can't remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 8th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: 8th of July. By virtue of that decision, 31st of July was set as the final date, implying that disclosure on the 8th of June and thereafter until the 31st of July would be regarded as timely. So the Defence point that 30 new witnesses had been introduced in the witness list along with its pre-trial -- along with the Prosecution's pre-trial brief on 8 June was too late because it -- many of those witnesses could actually have been chosen and indicated to the Defence much earlier. The Chamber's view is that, although the Defence might think and that might perceive that six weeks ahead of trial is very short time to familiarise itself with a great number of new witnesses and a great number of new exhibits, all amounting to some 20 per cent of the total material, if we understand that correctly, although this may seem to the Defence to be too short, nevertheless that is according to the rule. And as it turned out, the next and the final date that was set, namely, the 31st of July, in fact turned out also to be exactly six weeks before the start of the trial, which is why, to come to my conclusion, that we will regard as timely all disclosure that was made prior to the 31st July, including the 30 new -- 39 new witnesses and the great number of documents that came in. This leaves us, then, with what to do with the 50 documents that came in after 31st July. The Chamber's view here is that because of the fact that the Prosecution failed to apply for leave to have these things disclosed, we would ordinarily exclude it. That was our initial opinion, that simply you had failed to apply, and had you applied you would probably have been given leave but you didn't, so whatever came after 31st July, we're sorry, cannot be admitted. Now, that of course is made redundant by the fact that you didn't even seek to have it included in the 65 ter list. So what's the point of excluding it if it weren't going to get into the 65 ter list anyway? However, we also had to look at the question of whether by the late disclosure the Defence would in any way be prejudiced, and looking at the documents we found that some of it did attract some attention. Some of the proofing notes, for instance, I think -- even though the Prosecution would not intend to make any use of it, I would imagine, not having seen the documents so I don't know what we're talking about, but I imagine that at least some of the proofing notes might be something that the Defence would have an interest in seeing and possibly also the other -- some of the other documents. For this reason we have come to the conclusion that, for these 50 documents, the question is whether the late disclosure of them impacts on the Defence's possibility to cross-examine the witnesses that pertain to these 50 documents. And since we found that the Defence might possibly suffer some prejudice by having only late access to these materials, our determination at this point before we have heard the parties - and we are now asking the parties for their submissions, oral submissions, that is - our inclination is that we would postpone the calling of those witnesses to whom the 50 documents pertain for a period of two months, which is a little more than the six weeks otherwise required. So this -- the position of the Chamber is that because of the possible prejudice that the Defence might suffer from the late disclosure of the post-31st July documents, we would order the Prosecution not to call any witness to whom this material pertains before expiration of a period of two months from today. But before we take this decision we would like to hear the Prosecution and the Defence's views on this because we don't know just how many witnesses we're talking about. And so if I can ask Mrs. Korner to indicate the number of witnesses that will be affected and which witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say, first of all, that there are a number of different items relating to different witnesses. Does Your Honour have the schedule attached to the back of our filing? It's -- it was filed on the 2nd of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have it now. Thank you, Mrs. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honour looks at the first page of Confidential Annex A, Witness ST019 is likely to be an early witness, but what was not disclosed has absolutely no bearing at all on any of the evidence he's going to give or any issue in this trial. And indeed, there -- the documents not disclosed vary from witness to witness. And a blanket ruling such as that, Your Honour, may have problems. I can't at the moment because we can't work out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me be more clear, then, Mrs. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What we're saying is that if, for instance, the proofing note of a witness lies among the 50 late documents, in that case we don't think that it would be proper to call that witness until such time as the Defence has had ample time to look at it and to study it, and we just suggest two months from today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's proofing notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's proofing notes or statements or any other document that goes directly with the witness. I mean, I understand that some of the documents were also transcripts from domestic proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if a witness has given a statement before a national court in Serbia or in Bosnia or elsewhere, well, that witness you have to hold back until two months from today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, Your Honour, can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So proofing notes, statements, and other such direct material.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. In that case, Your Honour, at the moment can we reserve our submissions until we try to work out whether this would affect any witnesses that we were likely to call in the early stages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have an indication as to when you would provide us with that information? Thursday next week?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no. As soon as we've worked it out. It affects 32 -- these documents affected 32 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In a direct fashion?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, in a direct, very, very few. Two of them were only interviewed very recently, effectively to dispense with a late proofing note which -- so that's why it wasn't disclosed because it hasn't happened. We're trying, in the interests of efficiency, to see as many witnesses in advance to -- so the Defence knows exactly what they're going to say. I can't at the moment say whether it's going to affect any witnesses who we'd call within those two months, but we will inform the Court by the opening. Will that do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Monday is accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Submissions from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in a pretty awkward situation on this. The reason is the following. We have the list. We received the DVDs with the documentation. However, unfortunately, due to some electronic glitch it is unreadable and we returned them -- I mean, in a majority it is unreadable. It took me eight hours to download and finally it -- I couldn't work with it. Now, we at this point cannot say anything because we haven't seen the actual documents still. We hope we will receive them very soon from our friends from the Prosecution, I mean the actual DVDs. So then we can download the documents. Then we can review -- I'm not saying that Ms. Korner is wrong or I am -- I'm actually accepting what she's saying, but at least we would need to confirm that by our own eyes. Does it really -- does it really pertains to 50 witness statements? Does it really consider 36 witnesses or whatever is the number? So therefore in this sense we would not be able to give you any -- any -- any position at least from the Stanisic Defence until we review that. And if that would be the case, then at least we would like to be heard on the -- on that after we reviewed them. That's the unfortunate situation with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HICKS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, I have to echo the sentiments of Mr. Zecevic in that we have not been able to review the materials as well, due to much of the DVD portions being corrupted. We were able to see that there's 2.044 files included, which is a tremendous amount to review, and again, I just agree with Mr. Zecevic's comments. We -- I only spent seven hours trying to download it before it was -- realised that it was corrupted, but we're not in a position to give substantive comments on these documents at this stage either. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were told today that's the problem. We don't understand why because before we send it out we check it on our equipment and it plays, but something seems to go wrong when it gets to the Defence. But there is one other matter. Your Honour, we're still disclosing transcripts which we get back from the shorthand writers. We disclose the tapes, but as the Defence -- I think it was said at one stage you can't search a tape. So we're dependent on the shorthand writers here doing the transcripts. We're disclosing them. What I simply want to know is, is Your Honour saying that we need to ask your leave to hand over the transcripts each time? These are transcripts of interviews of witnesses which have been conducted. We've handed over the tapes so that they're in English and B/C/S on the tapes, because everything's recorded, particularly with insider witnesses. But the transcripts, as Your Honour knows because we've had a lot of discussion about it, there's -- I mean it's a complete backlog because nothing was happening over the summer break. So, are you saying we should ask your leave to disclose to the Defence what they're asking for? I know it sounds mad, but that's what it sounds as though Your Honour was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What I'm not clear about, Ms. Korner, is that -- and it may seem to be an odd question for the Bench to be asking you, but who's property is the transcripts? Aren't they the common property of the -- if they're product of the -- of the ordinary work of the Tribunal, I'm not sure why you -- the question of leave to hand them over would arise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no, no, this is -- but that's -- the reason I'm asking about that is because we have an obligation, whether it was beyond the 31st of July or not, to disclose any documents, any statements that we've overlooked or omitted to disclose in any event. But what I think is a slight confusion here is what Your Honours are getting at is you won't allow us to use or lead evidence in matters which are late disclosed. That, I think, must be the gravamen of this, because otherwise if we were told we couldn't disclose, well, then we'd be in breach of all the rules that says we must disclose to the Defence. It's the use, I think, which is -- Your Honours were aiming at. But it just sounded for a moment as though we were being told that had we applied for leave to late disclose copies of transcripts or whatever it was that we omitted to disclose, then we'd have got it. But we have to disclose. If we find documents which are relevant to witnesses we're calling or in some way assist the Defence, we have to disclose it. We are the owners of the original tapes of interviews with witnesses, which we then get transcribed. So the transcriptions, when done, come to us and we then give it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I now understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The context of your --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The problem which the Chamber sees -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour. On that very issue which is important also for my client, I just got a note, and with your permission if he can have few words with regard to this issue of disclosure and materials and the problems that he suffers with electronic equipment and opening the documents just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The accused speaks through his counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. It's very specific issue, so I'm not so sure that I am familiar with it. But the problem is that Mr. Zupljanin has a serious problem to open all these materials through his computer because the problem is in a programme called Roxio, like Romeo-Oscar-X-ray-India-Oscar, which is completely not fitting with these programmes that OTP is using. So just for the record, that maybe it's a matter of assistance of the Registry to deal with it. But we hope that it can be resolved soon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have come across these problems many, many times before, and the obvious solution of course is for the Prosecution, when it discloses material to Defence, to provide not only the material in an electronic form but also to provide the software needed for the Defence to be able to apply this material and to open it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They have it, apparently, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They have -- I'm told by Mr. Smith they have the software.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In that case I'm not sure I fully understand the problem any longer. But in any case, it's not a problem that we can settle here. If, Mr. Pantelic -- on your computer you need software installed to be able to open effectively the material you get from the Prosecution, then please contact the Registry or the UNDU and -- through your lawyer, and I'm sure that the problem can be fixed soon and I hope it can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, just before we leave and one last matter. It doesn't matter because everything -- those 50 documents were all -- fell within Rule 66(ii). But, Your Honour, Rule 66(ii), and Your Honour specifically mentioned it during the course of the Status Conference, I -- I think it was 65 ter, you said: "I also wanted to set a date in accordance with Rule 66(A)(ii) for the Prosecution to file copies of all transcripts and written statements." It -- that's exactly -- it doesn't actually include documents, exhibits. It's written statements it applies to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, but you -- Mrs. Korner, you will appreciate the fact that according to Rule 65 ter (E), you are required to provide copies of all documents other than statements by the time you submit your pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So there was no need to set -- you know, to mention that again. It was just in order to solve a practical problem that I proposed a date for the submission of the 66(A)(ii) material, but I think it was clearly understood by everyone that that would also include whatever possible documents that would come with that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're fully aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- so there was no doubt in my mind that 31st of July was the closing date and after that nothing, except with leave from the Pre-Trial Chamber. Your question to the Chamber was whether we would require -- whether you would have to ask for leave to file all further documents still not on your 65 ter list, and I think the rule is clear and simple. If you need to add documents to your 65 ter list, you need to apply for leave, yes. So that's the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's my fault, I'm sure. Your Honour said disclose -- and absolutely if we need to use further documents then we must apply. We understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. Right. I hope this brings us to the end of the agenda for today. We have a number of pending motions other than those that we have covered in this Pre-Trial Conference. Some of them, I think, relate to protective measures and there are other issues. I think at this late time what I should do is simply to restrict myself as to saying that the remaining pending motions will be dealt with very, very soon, hopefully before the opening of the trial, but if not then as soon as we can thereafter. And of course we are particularly sensitive to the issue of adjudicated facts. We hope to be able to render that decision -- I can't promise, but we are really working very, very hard to try and see if we can have it ready by the course of next week. But otherwise it will come very, very early.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But -- but, Your Honour, that's -- I was going to raise that and, indeed, raised it with Ms. Featherstone before. You've asked by Thursday to notify you of new witnesses or how we are going to reduce our witness list. We would simply say this: Without the decision on adjudicated facts it's even more difficult to make a proper decision, because once we know which facts you have found as adjudicated about which you would yet need more evidence, then we have a better idea of whom we can remove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, but you still would be able to make your final list. I agree that there would be some uncertainty, and if by delivery of our decision on adjudicated facts you wish to make any changes in your list at that time you can do so. But bear in mind that a number of adjudicated facts have already been admitted by the Pre-Trial Chamber when Mr. Stanisic was alone on the docket. So there's a couple of hundred adjudicated facts already that have been admitted in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, but, Your Honour, the -- in particular, the ones from the Krajisnik judgement cover areas which the other adjudicated facts did not. And, Your Honours, with the greatest of respect, it -- you know, to produce a revised witness list before we know what's going to be adjudicated facts, we submit, does make life even more complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but you have to try --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're not sympathetic in the slightest, I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, I'm not. We can try -- if that would be of particular use to you, we can try to see if we can deliver part of our decision on the adjudicated facts specifically relating to Krajisnik by Thursday --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, on the 24th of February of this year we filed a request for notice regarding the application of the adjudicated facts to Stojan Zupljanin. At the moment they're only in respect to Stanisic. Can we at least know perhaps that, whether you would be applying the same agreement of adjudicated facts in respect of Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It would be difficult now that the cases have been joined not to apply them to Zupljanin. So what was admitted for Stanisic will cover Zupljanin as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But we will -- maybe we will split up our decision on adjudicated facts, and if that is of particular importance to you, then seek to, in part, hand down our decision on the adjudicated facts in Krajisnik by the close of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HICKS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hicks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HICKS
utterances.text: Should we take that as a decision, an oral decision in regards to adjudicated facts as applicable to Mr. Zupljanin or will there be a written decision in this regard? Because we did reply to the Prosecution's notice in that regard and there has been no formal decision as of yet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I better be on the safe side and say we will provide a written decision. But as I recall, most of the adjudicated facts that relate to Mr. Stanisic are not immediately relevant to your client, but I need to check that. So there shouldn't be much difficulty for you in accepting the adjudicated facts that relate to Stanisic. Senor Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Grazie, Your Honour. I'm not so sure from the top of my head, but I think former lead counsel Mr. Bezbradica from Australia, who was lead counsel for Stanisic, accepted certain facts related to my client, Mr. Zupljanin, when -- during his period when he was at large so for various reasons. I know. So Mr. Zupljanin was not here in the case. And a lawyer, Bezbradica, simply in communication with the Prosecution, admitted. So obviously we have to go through this list that it's absolutely acceptable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that. In any case, we will hand down the decision in writing. I think this concludes the points on the agenda for this Pre-Trial Conference, and unless there are other matters that the parties wish to raise -- Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really kindly ask you to consider if I well understood that the beginning of trial is in the afternoon session of Monday, 14th of September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me ask the Registrar about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Registrar has informed me that the trial will begin on Monday, the 14th of September, at 2.15, in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's -- brings me, Your Honour, to my issue, small problem in general it is, but big for me for visa issue. I kindly ask if it is possible to remove afternoon session to morning session because it will be a great importance and honour for me to follow this opening statement in live. And then I have to catch a plane to leave Schengen territory before midnight and to then come on the 15 -- 15th of September in the morning. So just a small adjustment. Instead of afternoon session if it's possible to have morning session on 14th of September. And then on Tuesday instead of morning maybe afternoon. But it's afternoon -- for Tuesday -- so for Tuesday everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid that I'm very content with the afternoon session because I have problems over the weekend as well. So I -- as much as I'd like to help out Mr. Pantelic, if it's listed at 2.15, I would like it to stay at 2.15 on Monday. Or start on Tuesday, I don't mind which, but I don't -- I would have problems if it's transferred to the morning session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There might be a simple problem in that it simply isn't possible because if we have to switch with another trial, then that might be difficult for technical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But maybe, Your Honour -- sorry to interrupt in your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But before I give you the floor, Mr. Pantelic, I understand your reasons for wanting to observe the opening statements by the Prosecution; that is of course a crucial element in this case. However, what we normally do when we cannot be present is that we are provided with a CD-ROM with the audio-visual recordings of that session. So if you can't be here and if we can't move, and I understand that Mrs. Korner has a difficulty in moving, then the next-best thing would be to provide you with a CD to enable you to simply observe on a TV screen instead. It's not perfect but it's the best we can offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Or maybe, if it's possible, to postpone the opening from Monday to Tuesday, that would be a really great assistance, just one day, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I really would like to help you, but, as you have understood, we are really hard-pressed for time. If we have to close the Prosecution's case by the 1st of April, we don't have a minute to lose. I'm simply afraid of -- because we -- I'm afraid of losing one day of trial because it would imply that Donia could only come on Thursday then. And so the whole thing would be postponed for one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it would be Donia on Thursday and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so on, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The only option I see, Mrs. Korner, is if -- we could start on the Tuesday if you were able to tell us that you would only use one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I -- I know that but I -- this is our opportunity to explain our case properly and I think that that can't happen. But, Your Honour, I've just been passed a note that Your Honour's ruling of the postponement of two months would affect Donia. There was a proofing note apparently, one-page proofing note, but I know that both my friends over there are fully familiar with Dr. Donia -- and the other thing about proofing notes is if there was a proofing note, it meant the evidence was going to be given in the transcript, so it would be in the transcript. But I do hope that Your Honour won't rule that I can't call Dr. Donia because of a one-page proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I ask for an opinion by the -- would you accept that we can begin with Donia? Will you accept the dispensation with this one-page proofing note on Mr. Donia so that we can hear him rather than having to knock him off for two months?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I would love to accommodate you but I would need to see the note first. Maybe it's -- maybe it's irrelevant for us altogether, and then we might accommodate the Prosecution in that. But first we need to see -- that's our problem because we haven't been able to see any of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can read -- I can summarise this. He went to -- Dr. Donia told --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Rather than starting using up time here, could you provide a copy to the Defence teams right away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we can [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Why don't we do that, and then I would have to ask the Defence counsels if they would be good enough to give us a reply back Monday or Tuesday at the latest whether they are willing to dispense with this. It's ironic that our own order seems to run -- but given the fact that it is apparently a very small thing, I hope that we can solve it in a practical manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. We will do as you have suggested. There's one other thing. It was my understanding that our friends are asking for two days of the opening statement. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: One and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And they -- just a minute ago they suggested that Dr. Donia as the first witness is appearing on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If we were to accommodate Mr. Pantelic's wish --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- that would mean that we couldn't hear Dr. Donia on Wednesday but would have to put him off for Thursday --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thursday, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- and that would cost us one full day of trial which is only going to hit us in the end --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- so we won't be able to adjourn on April --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was my misunderstanding. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Any other issues that we wish to raise? Because I have the usual issue that I need to put to the two accused, and that is to ask about your conditions, your health conditions, and if there are any issues relating to your detention that you wish to raise with the Chamber at this moment. Mr. Stanisic, you may rise. THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] I have no objections to the conditions of detention. My health is good and if there are going to be any issues to be raised, we'll have opportunity to do that. But for the time being, I have nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that and I'm glad to hear that you are in good shape. Mr. Zupljanin, you may rise. THE ACCUSED ZUPLJANIN: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Harhoff, for having given me this opportunity to express our concerns. You know how life is in a detention unit. For the time being, conditionally put, things are fine, but I would to use this opportunity to say the following. Given that I spend most of my time now before a computer, due to the lack of time and the sheer volume of material I have to go through, I wanted to share this with you: I have lots of problems with opening CDs which had been burned in Roxio, a software. I would kindly ask that this issue be given sufficient attention. I don't know why so much stress is placed on us having to work with this software which is incompatible with many others. Perhaps this should be done in a compatible type of software compatible to Word, for example, otherwise we use a lot of time and end up with many useless CDs. As for any other conditions I have nothing in particular to say and I thank you for this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zupljanin. As I indicated earlier on during this meeting, I hope that the issues relating to your difficulties in opening the documents that you get from the Prosecution can be solved. Apparently it seems to work for most of the other accused, and so if there's any particular problem relating to your computer in particular, I'm sure that that can be resolved through the assistance of the Registry or the UNDU. But please raise it with your counsel and with the commander of the UNDU, and let's hope that this issue can be resolved. Am I to understand that you are otherwise in good health? THE ACCUSED ZUPLJANIN: [Interpretation] My health situation is pretty good. I live a sporty life. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. This concludes today's Pre-Trial Conference. I look forward to receiving the submissions that we have agreed on today and I look forward to seeing you all again on Monday, the 14th of September, at 2.15, in this courtroom for the opening statement of the Prosecution. Thank you very much. This meeting is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: adjourned at 5.44 p.m. 21 22 23 24
